tier_reason: First-party chart in the pogreb README ('Random lookup performance', reads/s vs number of keys) shows pogreb far ahead of goleveldb, bolt and badgerdb; benchmark code is public (akrylysov/pogreb-bench, cmd/pogreb-bench + kv/*.go) but there is no CPU model (only 'DigitalOcean 8 CPUs'), no Go version/flags and no run parameters, so C.

corrections.baseline: goleveldb (pure-Go port of LevelDB; the C++ LevelDB was not tested)
corrections.claimed_speedup: README chart (image only, no numeric table) shows pogreb random-lookup throughput of roughly 1.2M reads/s at 10K keys falling to roughly 0.7M reads/s at 10M keys, vs roughly 0.13M falling to 0.03M reads/s for goleveldb, i.e. about 10x at 10K keys to about 20x at 10M keys (approximate, read off the chart image; derived from page data); bolt and badgerdb are also well below pogreb at every key count.
corrections.workload: Random point lookups at 10K, 100K, 1M and 10M keys (chart x-axis) against goleveldb, bolt (bbolt) and badgerdb using akrylysov/pogreb-bench; the tool defaults are 16-64 B keys, 128-512 B values and 1 goroutine, but the README does not state which parameters produced the chart.
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as a chart image; the benchmark code lives in the separate first-party pogreb-bench repo (10 stars, last commit 2024-06-30), which contains no results. The chart dates from 2018-2019 (README Performance section added 2018-01-07; the image is served with Last-Modified 2019-09-24), so it predates pogreb's 2020 write-ahead-log redesign and uses old versions of every engine. The baseline is goleveldb, a Go port, not the C++ LevelDB. Only reads were benchmarked, and there is no CPU model, Go version or build flags. By design pogreb cannot do range scans.

notes: Numbers are real and favourable, but they come from a stale chart of pre-0.9 pogreb against goleveldb rather than LevelDB proper, so I pointed benchmark_url at the README section that holds the chart. The pogreb-bench URL holds only code. Metadata checks out (Apache-2.0, 1,350 stars, last commit 2026-04-06, not archived, not a fork).

tier_reason: The starskey-io/bench README lists first-party timings for Starskey, Pebble, BBolt, Badger, LMDB and RocksDB from public code (main.go for the Go engines, c/main.c for RocksDB/LMDB built with 'gcc ... -Wall', no -O level), but there is no CPU model ('crappy 4 year old system') and no Go flags, and the harness is not like-for-like, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page timings for 10,000 ops with 32-byte keys/values: Starskey write 53.3 ms, get 4.81 ms, delete 28.9 ms vs RocksDB 286.9 ms, 10.1 ms, 283.1 ms, i.e. about 5.4x write, 2.1x get and 9.8x delete (derived from page data). LMDB beats Starskey on every operation (3.74 ms / 2.00 ms / 3.40 ms), and BBolt beats it on get (4.56 ms) and delete (5.46 ms). The RocksDB gap is inflated by a mismatched harness (see caveats).
corrections.caveats: The harness is not like-for-like. Starskey's Put/Delete only append to the WAL and fsync in the background every 256 ms (default BackgroundFSync), while the bench syncs RocksDB (sync=1 and use_fsync=1), Pebble (pebble.Sync) and Badger (SyncWrites) on every op, despite the code comment claiming Starskey 'syncs to disk automatically'. BBolt and LMDB batch all ops in one transaction. RocksDB/LMDB are timed with C clock() (process CPU time), whereas the Go engines use wall-clock time.Since. Hardware is unstated beyond a 'crappy 4 year old system'; there are no Go build flags and the C harness has no -O level. On the page's own numbers LMDB beats Starskey on every operation and BBolt beats it on get and delete, so 'faster than incumbents' holds only against per-op-fsync RocksDB. The bench pins starskey v0.1.8 (latest tag v0.1.9).

notes: Every number matches the bench README, but the win over RocksDB compares background-fsync Starskey with per-op-fsync RocksDB timed by CPU clock, so I downgraded the claim (tier stays C). Metadata checks out (MPL-2.0, 161 stars, last commit 2025-03-19 = stale, not archived, not a fork).
